```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(bst260projhelp)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
have_dt <- requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)
dtab <- function(d, ...) if (have_dt) DT::datatable(d, ...) else d
```

The other two vignettes work from PDF reports. This one works from a
journal article published only as HTML -- a PMC page bundled with the
package -- and shows a third kind of information transformation:
`rvest`-based scraping instead of `pdftools`-based extraction.

```{r}
article <- bst260_example("PMC13794488.html")
```

## Information transformation: scraping structure out of PMC's HTML

PMC renders every article against the same handful of conventions:
standard `citation_*` meta tags in the `<head>` (the Highwire
Press/Google Scholar scheme most publishing platforms emit), and
predictable element ids in the body (`TabN` for tables, `FigN` for
figures, `AbsN` for the abstract, `CRN` for reference-list entries).
None of the functions below are specific to this one paper -- they
read those conventions, not anything peculiar to this article.

### Article metadata, straight from the `<head>`

```{r}
meta <- html_article_meta(article)
meta[c("title", "journal", "volume", "date", "doi", "pmid")]
meta$authors
```

### Finding and reading a table

Unlike a PDF, where a table has no machine-readable boundary and has
to be found by its caption text, an HTML table is a real `<table>`
element -- but it still needs to be found correctly: PMC wraps each
table together with its caption in an enclosing `<section>`, and
calling `rvest::html_table()` on *that* wrapper (rather than drilling
down to the actual `<table>` inside it) silently produces a nonsense
one-row pseudo-table instead of erroring. `html_table_index()` lists
what's there; `html_read_table()` does the drill-down correctly:

```{r}
html_table_index(article)[c("id", "label")]
```

Table 2 reports the paper's own segmented-regression estimates, and
its column names are the paper's abbreviations, not self-explanatory
labels, so they're worth spelling out before the table appears rather
than after:

- **change point** -- the year, estimated from the data rather than
  assumed, at which the trend in mortality significantly shifts.
- **APC** (annual percentage change) -- the constant yearly rate of
  change *within* one segment of the trend (e.g. before vs. after the
  change point).
- **AAPC** (average annual percentage change) -- a single summary rate
  across the *whole* 1999-2023 period, averaging the early- and
  late-period APCs in proportion to how many years each segment spans.

```{r}
tab2 <- html_read_table(article, "Tab2")
dtab(tab2)
```

### Abstract and a cited figure

```{r}
ab <- html_abstract(article)
names(ab)
ab[["Background"]]
```

Figures are harder to extract "as text" than tables are, since the
data they summarize was never in the HTML at all -- but the image
itself is: PMC serves it from its own CDN, so `html_figure_image()`
just needs the `<img>` element's `src`, not a download. `article` is
licensed CC BY 4.0 (confirmed below, straight from the page's own
licence statement), so it can be reproduced here with attribution
rather than only described:

```{r}
fig1 <- html_figure_image(article, "Fig1")
knitr::include_graphics(fig1$src)
```

```{r, results = "asis"}
cap <- html_figure_caption(article, "Fig1")
meta <- html_article_meta(article)
cat(sprintf(
  "**Fig. 1.** %s\n\n*Source:* %s. %s. *%s*. %s;%s:%s. [%s](https://doi.org/%s). Licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).",
  cap, paste(meta$authors, collapse = ", "), meta$title, meta$journal,
  substr(meta$date, 1, 4), meta$volume, meta$firstpage, meta$doi, meta$doi
))
```

Both the table- and figure-extraction functions above are generic in
the same sense the PDF ones are: nothing about them is specific to
stroke, diabetes, or this journal -- the same calls work on any PMC
article that follows these id and meta-tag conventions.

## Bibliographic integrity: a reference list PMC has already structured

This paper cites by number -- `[1]`, `[1, 2]` -- against a 21-entry
reference list. Unlike the RAND and CDC reports, where the reference
list is plain PDF text that first has to be parsed back into
structure, PMC's own HTML has already done that: each entry is a
`<li id="CRN">` carrying a formatted citation plus direct links to its
DOI and PubMed record, and every in-text citation marker is itself a
real link, `<a href="#CRN">`, straight to its entry -- not text that
merely looks like a citation. So `pmc_ref_entries()` and
`pmc_find_citations()` are reads, not parsers:

```{r}
refs <- pmc_ref_entries(article)
nrow(refs)
refs[1:3, c("key", "text", "doi")]

cites <- pmc_find_citations(article)
nrow(cites)
head(cites)
```

### Cross-checking the citations

Because every in-text marker is already a structural link, checking
that it resolves to a real entry is just a set-membership test -- no
heuristic regex over plain text, the way
[vancouver_find_numeric_citations()] has to work:

```{r}
stopifnot(all(cites$key %in% refs$key))
```

Each citation link gets its own anchor id, via the same
[bib_cite_link()] used for the RAND and CDC vignettes, so it can link
down to its entry and that entry can link back up to every place it
was cited:

```{r}
cite_id <- paste0("cite-", cites$key, "-", seq_len(nrow(cites)))
cites$link <- bib_cite_link(cites$key, label = cites$label, id = cite_id)
cited_at <- split(cite_id, cites$key)
dtab(cites[c("para", "key", "link")], escape = FALSE)
```

### The rendered bibliography

`pmc_bibliography_html()` is a thin wrapper around the same
[bib_html_list()] renderer the RAND and CDC vignettes use -- PMC's
entries arrive already formatted with their own DOI and a PubMed
fallback URL, so there's no formatting step first. Every entry links
to its DOI on `doi.org`; the small `&uarr;` links back up to every
place in the text it was actually cited:

```{r, results = "asis"}
cat(pmc_bibliography_html(refs, cited_at), sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
table(has_doi = !is.na(refs$doi))
```

Most entries have a DOI linked directly in PMC's own HTML, but not
all -- a handful (e.g. government data-brief and surveillance-report
citations) have neither a DOI nor a PubMed record, and are correctly
marked `no DOI` above rather than silently dropped, the same guarantee
[bib_html_list()] makes for the RAND and CDC vignettes.
